name: LTIMindtree
tagline: Hires graduate/associate trainees through a proctored online test that gates technical and HR interviews, with a separate premium track for stronger coders.
timeline: Online test → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: A multi-section online test shortlists candidates, sometimes followed by an AI-bot video screen, then a technical interview and an HR round. The test is the main filter.

rounds.t: English, quant, logical reasoning, CS fundamentals, 1–2 coding problems
Self-intro, project walkthrough, a simple coding task; sometimes used to decide premium package
Resume language, DSA, OS, DBMS, project depth
Communication, relocation, motivation, fit

eligibility: Commonly 60% or 6.0 CGPA across 10th, 12th, and degree (B.E./B.Tech/MCA), no active backlogs at joining, gap usually not more than 2 years. Exact cutoffs vary by drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Rebuild quant and logical reasoning speed with timed sets
Days 4–6: Drill easy–medium coding (arrays, strings, hashing) in your main language
Days 7–9: Revise DBMS/SQL and OS core topics
Days 10–12: Prepare a crisp project story and resume-based answers
Days 13–14: Two full timed mock tests plus a mock technical + HR round
prepC: Day 1: Timed aptitude set plus 8–10 easy coding problems and SQL basics
Day 2: Revise OS/DBMS one-liners, rehearse intro and project pitch, do one mock

faq.q: Is the online test the main filter?
faq.a: Yes. Candidate reports consistently say clearing the multi-section online test is the hardest gate; most rejections happen there before interviews.

faq.q: What is the AI/bot round about?
faq.a: Some drives use an AI-proctored video screen for a self-introduction, project talk, and a small coding task. It is sometimes tied to eligibility for a higher salary band.

faq.q: Do I need advanced DSA?
faq.a: For the standard track, easy–medium problems are enough. The premium/higher-package track expects stronger coding, so aim higher if you want that band.

name: Mphasis
tagline: Recruits associate software engineers via an aptitude/coding test, a combined technical-HR interview, and a spoken-English (Versant) check.
timeline: Online test → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: An online test (often AMCAT-style) covering aptitude and programming leads to a technical plus HR interview and a Versant spoken-English assessment; some drives add a group discussion.

rounds.t: Logical reasoning, quant, verbal ability, computer programming
Communication and interpersonal skills
CS fundamentals, coding basics, projects, communication and fit
Pass/fail spoken-English fluency

eligibility: Typically 60% or ~6.3 CGPA in graduation with no current backlogs (Maharashtra candidates sometimes accepted from ~55%). Good communication and location flexibility expected. Varies by drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude drills across logical, quant, and verbal
Days 4–6: Programming MCQs and easy coding problems
Days 7–9: Revise OOP, DBMS, and OS basics
Days 10–11: Practice spoken English aloud daily for the Versant round
Days 12–14: Mock GD, mock technical+HR, and one full test
prepC: Day 1: Timed aptitude set plus programming MCQs and 6–8 easy coding problems
Day 2: Speak English aloud in mock answers, revise OOP/DBMS, rehearse intro

faq.q: What is the Versant round?
faq.a: It is an automated spoken-English test scored for fluency and pronunciation. Treat it as pass/fail and practice speaking clearly aloud beforehand.

faq.q: Is there always a group discussion?
faq.a: No. Reports say GD appears in some campus drives and is skipped in others, so prepare for it but do not assume it.

faq.q: How hard is the coding section?
faq.a: It is basic. Focus on writing correct, simple programs rather than advanced algorithms.

name: Persistent Systems
tagline: Puts more weight on coding than most peers, with an aptitude/coding test, an advanced coding round, and technical plus HR interviews.
timeline: Online test → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: An online test (often AMCAT-style with aptitude and technical) is followed by an advanced coding round for shortlisted candidates, then technical interviews and an HR round; some candidates enter via the Martian training program.

rounds.t: Logical/verbal aptitude, puzzles, OOP/DBMS/networking/DS, easy–medium coding
Harder coding problems for qualified candidates
Language proficiency, OOP, SQL, DSA, problem solving, projects
Behavioral questions and fit

eligibility: Open to B.E./B.Tech across CSE, IT, ECE, and related branches; specific CGPA/percentage cutoffs vary by drive. Confirm each drive's notification.
prep2: Days 1–3: Rebuild aptitude and puzzle-solving speed
Days 4–7: Daily easy–medium coding on arrays, strings, recursion, sorting
Days 8–10: Revise OOP, DBMS/SQL, and networking basics
Days 11–12: Attempt harder coding to prepare for the advanced round
Days 13–14: Full mock test plus mock technical and HR
prepC: Day 1: 10–12 coding problems (easy→medium) plus core OOP/DBMS revision
Day 2: Timed aptitude, 3–4 harder problems, rehearse project explanation

faq.q: How coding-heavy is Persistent?
faq.a: More than typical service companies. Beyond the first test there is often an advanced coding round, so practice medium-level problems, not just aptitude.

faq.q: What is the Martian Program?
faq.a: It is a training-and-internship path where selected freshers learn core tech (Java, MySQL, Linux) before final evaluation. Entry still starts with an online assessment.

faq.q: Which language should I use?
faq.a: Use the one you know best (C++, Java, or Python) and be ready to answer OOP and SQL questions in the interview.

name: Coforge
tagline: Hires Graduate Engineer Trainees via a Mettl-based assessment (aptitude, coding, verbal) followed by technical and HR interviews.
timeline: Assessment → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: Applications are screened, then a Mettl online assessment covering aptitude, coding, and verbal shortlists candidates for one or more technical interviews and a final HR round.

rounds.t: Aptitude, logical reasoning, quant, coding, verbal
Core CS, coding/scenario problems, project depth
Communication, motivation, cultural fit

eligibility: Open to B.E./B.Tech, MCA, and M.Tech; Coforge does not always publish a fixed CGPA/percentage cutoff, so a strong academic record and projects help. Varies by drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude and logical reasoning practice
Days 4–6: Easy–medium coding in your main language
Days 7–9: Revise OOP, DBMS, and CS fundamentals
Days 10–12: Practice scenario/problem-solving questions and polish resume
Days 13–14: Full mock assessment plus mock technical and HR
prepC: Day 1: Timed aptitude plus 8–10 coding problems and verbal practice
Day 2: Revise OOP/DBMS, rehearse project story and one mock interview

faq.q: Which platform is the test on?
faq.a: Reports say the online assessment is typically conducted on Mettl and includes aptitude, coding, and verbal sections.

faq.q: Is there a fixed CGPA cutoff?
faq.a: Not always published. Coforge often weighs overall profile, projects, and problem solving rather than a single strict number, but always check the drive notification.

faq.q: How selective is the shortlist?
faq.a: In some campus drives only a couple hundred of roughly a thousand applicants reach interviews, so the assessment is the key filter.

name: Hexaware
tagline: Runs an all-elimination Graduate Engineer Trainee funnel: aptitude, technical MCQs, a coding round, then HR.
timeline: Assessment → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: A four-stage elimination process: an aptitude test, a technical MCQ section, a coding round, and an HR interview. Each round must be cleared to advance.

rounds.t: Quant, verbal ability, logical reasoning (typically 60 questions, no negative marking)
CS fundamentals
Practical coding at easy–medium level
Behavioral and cultural fit

eligibility: Commonly 60% aggregate or 6.0 CGPA with no active backlogs; GET roles often open to CSE, IT, ECE, EEE, and Mechanical. Confirm the exact cutoff in each drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Timed aptitude across quant, verbal, and logical
Days 4–6: Technical MCQ revision (OS, DBMS, OOP)
Days 7–10: Daily easy–medium coding practice
Days 11–12: Prepare HR/behavioral answers and resume
Days 13–14: Full mock funnel end to end
prepC: Day 1: Aptitude set plus technical MCQ revision
Day 2: 8–10 coding problems and rehearse HR answers

faq.q: Are all rounds elimination?
faq.a: Yes. Each stage is qualifying, so you must clear aptitude, technical MCQ, and coding before the HR round.

faq.q: Is there negative marking in aptitude?
faq.a: Reports indicate the aptitude section (around 60 questions in 60 minutes) has no negative marking, so attempt everything.

faq.q: How hard is the coding round?
faq.a: Generally easy–medium (LeetCode-easy to medium range). Solid fundamentals and one language are enough.

name: Zensar
tagline: Uses a four-round funnel of online test, group discussion, technical interview, and HR, with GD sometimes skipped off-campus.
timeline: Online test → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: An online aptitude/technical test shortlists candidates for a group discussion (in some drives), followed by a technical interview and an HR round.

rounds.t: General aptitude, logical reasoning, verbal, sometimes technical MCQs
Communication and interpersonal skills
Coding, core CS concepts, problem solving
Soft skills, goals, cultural fit

eligibility: Typically 60% and above in Class X, XII, and B.Tech with no backlogs during the interview process. Varies by drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude, logical reasoning, and verbal practice
Days 4–6: Basic coding and CS concept revision
Days 7–9: Practice group-discussion topics aloud
Days 10–12: Mock technical interview and project prep
Days 13–14: Full mock test plus mock GD and HR
prepC: Day 1: Timed aptitude set plus CS concept revision
Day 2: One GD topic aloud, basic coding, and a mock interview

faq.q: Is the group discussion always held?
faq.a: No. GD appears in many campus drives but off-campus drives sometimes skip it. Prepare for it just in case.

faq.q: How technical is the online test?
faq.a: It is mostly aptitude (around 50 questions) with logical, quant, and verbal, and sometimes a technical MCQ section.

faq.q: What matters in the HR round?
faq.a: Communication, clarity on goals, and cultural fit. It is not a deep technical round.

name: Birlasoft
tagline: Runs a three-to-four round process: an online test with coding/technical/aptitude, then technical and HR interviews.
timeline: Assessment → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: Applications are screened, then an online test covering coding, technical, and aptitude shortlists candidates for a technical interview and an HR round.

rounds.t: Aptitude (~25 questions), technical (Java/C++/JavaScript/React), a simple coding question
C, C++, Java, SQL, core concepts, projects
Personality, background, interests, general fit

eligibility: Commonly minimum 60% across academics with a 6.0 CGPA and above, no backlogs, and academic gap usually not more than 1 year; graduates/postgraduates with a maths background. Varies by drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude practice (time and work, speed, distance)
Days 4–6: Java/C++ and SQL revision
Days 7–9: Simple coding practice
Days 10–12: Brush up JavaScript/React if relevant and prepare projects
Days 13–14: Full mock test plus mock technical and HR
prepC: Day 1: Timed aptitude plus Java/C++/SQL revision
Day 2: A few coding problems and rehearse project and HR answers

faq.q: How many aptitude questions are there?
faq.a: Reports mention roughly 25 aptitude questions with a generous time window, so accuracy matters more than speed here.

faq.q: Which languages are tested in interviews?
faq.a: Candidates report C, C++, Java, and SQL come up most often; be comfortable with basics and simple queries.

faq.q: Does the gap year rule matter?
faq.a: Often yes. Many drives ask for academic gaps of no more than about a year, so check your drive's notification.

name: Deloitte (India)
tagline: Runs a 4–5 stage funnel with a sectioned online assessment (including situational judgment) and multiple interviews up to partner level.
timeline: Assessment → interviews (3–5 weeks)
process: An online assessment covering aptitude, technical MCQs, and situational judgment leads to a technical interview, an HR/behavioral round, and often a final partner/director interview.

rounds.t: Quant/logical/verbal aptitude, technical MCQs and code snippets, situational judgment
Core subjects, projects, case-style problem solving
Behavioral questions, teamwork, communication
Leadership fit and alignment with values

eligibility: Commonly more than 60% in 10th, 12th, and graduation (full-time B.E./B.Tech/M.E./MCA). Fresher tracks include Business Technology Analyst and Associate Analyst Trainee. Varies by role and drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude across quant, logical, and verbal
Days 4–6: Technical MCQs, code snippets, and DSA basics
Days 7–8: Practice situational-judgment questions
Days 9–11: Prepare STAR-format behavioral stories and project talk
Days 12–14: Full mock assessment plus mock technical and behavioral rounds
prepC: Day 1: Timed aptitude plus technical MCQs and situational-judgment practice
Day 2: Prepare 3–4 STAR stories and rehearse project explanation

faq.q: What is the situational judgment section?
faq.a: It presents workplace scenarios and asks how you would respond. There is no code involved; answer in line with professionalism, teamwork, and client focus.

faq.q: Is there really a partner round?
faq.a: For many roles yes. A final partner/director interview checks culture fit and leadership potential rather than coding.

faq.q: Which fresher profiles exist?
faq.a: Reports cite Business Technology Analyst and Associate Analyst Trainee among the common engineering-fresher tracks, with content varying by service line.

name: EY (India)
tagline: Hires analysts and tech roles (including GDS) via an online assessment, an optional case/GD, technical rounds, and an HR/partner interview.
timeline: Assessment → interviews (3–5 weeks)
process: An online cognitive assessment leads to a group discussion or case exercise (conditional on volume), one or two technical/case interviews, and an HR or partner round on values fit.

rounds.t: Quant, verbal, and logical reasoning, sometimes a programming MCQ section
Reasoning, communication, structured thinking
Consulting frameworks, domain/technology concepts, problem solving
Fit and alignment with EY values

topics: CS or domain fundamentals for your role
eligibility: Commonly 60% and above in 10th, 12th, and graduation with no active backlogs; open across CSE, IT, ECE, EEE and non-tech streams depending on track. Varies by role and drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude across quant, verbal, and logical
Days 4–6: Case/structured-thinking basics
Days 7–8: Role-specific fundamentals (tech or domain)
Days 9–11: GD practice and STAR behavioral stories
Days 12–14: Full mock assessment plus mock case and HR rounds
prepC: Day 1: Timed aptitude plus one case-thinking walkthrough
Day 2: Prepare STAR stories, revise role fundamentals, and rehearse a GD topic

faq.q: Is there a group discussion?
faq.a: It is conditional. EY often includes a GD or case exercise but drops it depending on applicant volume, so prepare for it but do not rely on it.

faq.q: What are the fresher tracks?
faq.a: Broadly Analyst/Associate roles (consulting, audit, tax, business analysis) and technology roles (IT, cybersecurity, AI/ML, cloud), including GDS positions.

faq.q: How do I prepare for the partner/HR round?
faq.a: Focus on why-EY, values alignment, and clear communication. Have STAR-format examples of teamwork and problem solving ready.

name: KPMG (India)
tagline: Runs a 4–6 stage process; engineering freshers usually enter Advisory's tech/analytics practice via an aptitude test then technical and HR interviews.
timeline: Assessment → interviews (3–5 weeks)
process: An online aptitude assessment leads to an optional group discussion or case, then a technical interview on core CS and an HR interview on client-facing communication. Stage count varies by service line.

rounds.t: Numerical, verbal, and logical reasoning
Communication and structured thinking
Core CS concepts and projects
Communication under client-facing pressure and fit

eligibility: Commonly minimum 60% aggregate or equivalent CGPA with no active backlogs at joining; B.E./B.Tech/M.Tech/MCA in CS/IT/ECE for tech roles, though thresholds vary by business unit and drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude practice across numerical, verbal, and logical
Days 4–6: Core CS revision
Days 7–8: Analytics/data basics if targeting GTA
Days 9–11: GD practice and STAR stories
Days 12–14: Full mock assessment plus mock technical and HR
prepC: Day 1: Timed aptitude plus core CS revision
Day 2: One GD topic, STAR stories, and a mock interview

faq.q: Which practice do engineering freshers join?
faq.a: Reports say campus engineering freshers most often enter Advisory's Global Technology and Analytics (GTA) practice.

faq.q: Do non-engineering grads have a different path?
faq.a: Yes. B.Com and BBA graduates typically enter Audit and Tax tracks with different interview content from the tech track.

faq.q: How many rounds should I expect?
faq.a: Roughly 4–6 depending on role and program; the exact count and whether a GD or case is included varies by service line and drive.

name: PwC (India)
tagline: Runs a structured multi-stage graduate pipeline that can include a pre-recorded video interview and an assessment centre with group exercises.
timeline: Assessment → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: After screening, an online aptitude plus technical assessment leads to interviews; some graduate programs add a pre-recorded video interview and a virtual assessment centre with group and case exercises before final interviews.

rounds.t: Logical and verbal aptitude, technical concepts (OOP, DBMS, networking, DSA, .NET)
Pre-recorded responses to set questions
Group exercises, presentations, case studies
Core concepts and projects
Fit and alignment with PwC values

eligibility: Commonly 60% or 6.0 CGPA throughout academics with no active backlogs; B.E./B.Tech/M.Tech/MCA across branches. Varies by role and drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude across logical and verbal
Days 4–6: OOP, DBMS, networking, and DSA revision
Days 7–8: Practice recorded-video answers to common questions
Days 9–11: Case/group-exercise practice and STAR stories
Days 12–14: Full mock assessment plus mock technical and HR
prepC: Day 1: Timed aptitude plus core technical revision
Day 2: Record and review a mock video interview, prepare STAR stories and case basics

faq.q: What is the video interview like?
faq.a: For some graduate programs it is pre-recorded: you answer set questions on camera within a time limit, with no live interviewer. Practice speaking to a webcam beforehand.

faq.q: What happens at the assessment centre?
faq.a: It is a virtual session with group exercises, presentations, and case studies to gauge teamwork, problem solving, and leadership.

faq.q: Is the process the same for every role?
faq.a: No. Not all roles include the video and assessment-centre stages. The full five-stage pipeline mainly applies to structured graduate programs.

name: IBM India
tagline: Hires associate system/software engineers through a coding plus English online test, sometimes a GD, then technical and HR interviews.
timeline: Online test → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: An online assessment combining aptitude, coding, and an English test shortlists candidates, sometimes with a group discussion, followed by technical and HR interviews. Each round is qualifying.

rounds.t: Aptitude, coding, and English/cognitive sections
Teamwork and communication
Coding, design patterns, CS theory, projects
Cultural fit and communication

eligibility: Commonly minimum 60% or 6.0 CGPA with no active backlogs (some listings ask 65% in graduation/post-graduation); B.E./B.Tech in CSE/IT and related branches, often across recent batches. Varies by drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude and English/cognitive practice
Days 4–7: Daily coding in your main language (arrays, strings, DSA)
Days 8–10: CS fundamentals and design-pattern basics
Days 11–12: Communication and GD practice
Days 13–14: Full mock test plus mock technical and HR
prepC: Day 1: Timed aptitude/English plus 8–10 coding problems
Day 2: CS fundamentals revision, one GD topic, and a mock interview

faq.q: Is there an English test?
faq.a: Yes. IBM's online assessment commonly includes an English/cognitive component alongside coding, so practice clear written and spoken communication.

faq.q: Which languages are accepted for coding?
faq.a: Reports mention Java, C++, Python, and Node.js among preferred languages. Use the one you are strongest in.

faq.q: Is every round elimination?
faq.a: Yes. Each stage is qualifying, so you advance only after clearing the current one.

name: Oracle (India)
tagline: Product-company hiring with a higher bar: a coding-heavy online test, resume-driven technical rounds, and strong emphasis on SQL and databases.
timeline: Online test → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: A 90–120 minute online assessment with coding and technical concepts shortlists candidates for one or more technical interviews, often a managerial/scenario round, and an HR interview.

rounds.t: Aptitude, logical, verbal, 2–3 coding problems, SQL, DBMS/OOP basics
Coding, SQL queries, DSA, resume projects
Technical plus scenario-based judgment
Communication, personality, fit

eligibility: Commonly a stronger bar around 7.0 CGPA or 70% with good academics and solid SQL/database fundamentals. Varies by drive and role.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude plus SQL query practice
Days 4–7: Daily medium-level DSA/coding problems
Days 8–10: DBMS and OOP deep revision
Days 11–12: Resume-project prep and scenario thinking
Days 13–14: Full mock test plus mock technical and managerial rounds
prepC: Day 1: 10–12 coding problems plus intensive SQL practice
Day 2: DBMS/OOP revision and a mock technical interview on projects

faq.q: Is SQL really important?
faq.a: Yes. Oracle is a database company, so SQL queries and DBMS fundamentals come up heavily in both the test and interviews.

faq.q: How high is the CGPA bar?
faq.a: Reports suggest a stronger cutoff, often around 7.0 CGPA or 70%, higher than typical service companies. Confirm your drive's exact criteria.

faq.q: How hard is the coding?
faq.a: Expect roughly medium-level problems (2–3 in the test) plus follow-up optimization in interviews, so practice beyond easy problems.

name: SAP Labs India
tagline: Product-company process (e.g. Scholar@SAP) with an aptitude/coding test, two technical rounds, a managerial discussion, and an HR screen.
timeline: Online test → interviews (3–5 weeks)
process: An online assessment mixing aptitude and 1–2 coding problems leads to two technical interviews (heavy on Java/C++ and SQL), a managerial discussion, and an HR screen.

rounds.t: Maths, reasoning, verbal, CS fundamentals, 2 coding problems
Java/C++, DSA, SQL queries
Deeper coding, problem solving, projects
Design/scenario reasoning and approach
Communication and fit

eligibility: Commonly BE/B.Tech/ME/M.Tech/MCA with 60% or above in 10th, 12th, and graduation, no active backlogs at application, and a maximum education gap of about one year. Varies by drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude and reasoning practice
Days 4–7: Daily medium-level DSA and Java/C++ coding
Days 8–10: SQL, DBMS, and OS revision
Days 11–12: Design/scenario reasoning and project prep
Days 13–14: Two full mock technical rounds plus a mock managerial round
prepC: Day 1: 10–12 coding problems (Java/C++) plus SQL practice
Day 2: DBMS/OS revision, project prep, and a mock technical interview

faq.q: How many interview rounds are there?
faq.a: Reports describe up to five stages: the online test, two technical interviews, a managerial discussion, and an HR screen.

faq.q: Which languages should I focus on?
faq.a: Java and C++ are tested most, and SQL queries are standard in the first technical round.

faq.q: Can off-campus candidates apply?
faq.a: Yes. SAP runs on-campus drives across many colleges, and students from non-listed colleges can apply for off-campus roles via the SAP Careers portal.

name: Amdocs
tagline: Hires SDEs via a multi-section online test (aptitude, technical, coding) followed by technical and HR interviews.
timeline: Online test → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: A written/online test with aptitude, English, technical, and coding sections shortlists candidates for a technical interview and an HR round.

rounds.t: Quant, English, technical (Unix/SQL/OS/C outputs), 2–3 coding problems
DBMS, data structures (trees/traversal), language concepts, projects
Personality, communication, strengths/weaknesses, fit

eligibility: Specific CGPA/percentage cutoffs vary by drive; strong academics, no backlogs, and good communication help. Confirm each drive's notification.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude and English practice
Days 4–6: SQL/PL-SQL, Unix, and C-output questions
Days 7–9: OS and DBMS plus data-structure basics
Days 10–12: Coding practice and project prep
Days 13–14: Full mock test plus mock technical and HR
prepC: Day 1: Timed aptitude plus SQL/Unix/C-output practice
Day 2: Data-structure and DBMS revision, coding, and a mock interview

faq.q: What technical topics come up in the test?
faq.a: Reports mention Unix, SQL/PL-SQL, operating systems, and C output-prediction questions alongside the coding section.

faq.q: How many coding problems are there?
faq.a: Typically 2–3 in the online test, at a basic-to-moderate level.

faq.q: What does the technical interview focus on?
faq.a: DBMS, data structures (including trees and traversal), language concepts, and your projects.

name: DXC Technology
tagline: Uses a webcam-proctored AMCAT-style test (with essay writing and Automata Fix) followed by technical and HR interviews.
timeline: Assessment → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: After a pre-placement step, a webcam-proctored online test (numeracy, English/essay, logical reasoning, IT, Automata Fix) shortlists candidates for a technical interview and an HR interview.

rounds.t: Numeracy, English comprehension + essay, logical reasoning, IT, Automata Fix
OS, OOP, basic data structures, applied tech knowledge
Behavioral questions and personality fit

eligibility: Commonly B.E./B.Tech with 60% marks. Confirm exact cutoffs and eligible branches in each drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Numeracy and logical reasoning practice
Days 4–5: English comprehension and timed essay writing
Days 6–8: IT fundamentals and Automata Fix (debugging) practice
Days 9–11: OS, OOP, and basic data-structure revision
Days 12–14: Full mock test plus mock technical and HR
prepC: Day 1: Timed AMCAT-style set plus one practice essay
Day 2: Automata Fix debugging, OS/OOP revision, and a mock interview

faq.q: What is Automata Fix?
faq.a: It is a debugging section where you fix bugs in given code rather than write it from scratch. Practice reading and correcting code.

faq.q: Is there really an essay?
faq.a: Yes. The DXC test typically includes at least one essay-writing question, so practice writing clearly under time pressure.

faq.q: Is the test proctored?
faq.a: Reports indicate the AMCAT-based test is webcam-proctored, so take it in a quiet, well-lit setting alone.

name: Virtusa
tagline: Runs a long online test (MCQs plus two coding rounds) then one to two technical interviews, an optional GD, and HR.
timeline: Online test → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: A lengthy online test with MCQ sections and one to two coding rounds shortlists candidates for technical interviews, an optional group discussion, and an HR round.

rounds.t: 3 MCQ sections plus 1–2 coding rounds (easy–medium, then advanced)
OOP (Java/Python), SQL, data structures, projects
Communication and reasoning
Cultural fit and career goals

eligibility: Commonly minimum 60% aggregate across 10th, 12th, and graduation, no active backlogs, and at most about a one-year education gap. Varies by drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude MCQ practice
Days 4–7: Easy–medium coding building up to harder problems
Days 8–10: OOP, SQL, and data-structure revision
Days 11–12: GD practice and project prep
Days 13–14: Full timed mock test (including coding) plus mock interviews
prepC: Day 1: Timed MCQ set plus 10–12 coding problems (easy→advanced)
Day 2: OOP/SQL revision, one GD topic, and a mock technical interview

faq.q: How long is the online test?
faq.a: Reports say it can run around three hours, with three MCQ sections and one to two coding rounds, so build endurance for a long sitting.

faq.q: How hard is the coding?
faq.a: The first coding round is easy–medium; a second round, when present, includes advanced-level problems. Practice both tiers.

faq.q: Is the GD mandatory?
faq.a: No. It appears in some campus drives but not all. Prepare for it as a possibility.

name: Cyient
tagline: Engineering-focused hiring across many branches, with a role-dependent online assessment then technical and HR interviews.
timeline: Assessment → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: After application screening, a role-dependent online assessment (aptitude, coding, or technical) shortlists candidates for a technical interview and an HR round. Many hires come through campus drives and walk-ins.

rounds.t: Aptitude, logical reasoning, and role-specific coding/technical questions
Programming/engineering concepts, technical skills, problem solving
Communication, teamwork, adaptability, goals, fit

eligibility: Commonly a consistent academic record of 60% or more across BE/B.Tech/ME/M.Tech/MCA; eligible streams span Mechanical, ECE, EEE/E&I, Aeronautical, Civil, CS/IT, and Telecom. Varies by drive.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude and logical reasoning practice
Days 4–6: Role-specific fundamentals (software or core engineering)
Days 7–9: Basic coding or domain problem solving
Days 10–12: Resume and project prep plus communication practice
Days 13–14: Full mock assessment plus mock technical and HR
prepC: Day 1: Timed aptitude plus role-specific concept revision
Day 2: A few coding/domain problems, project prep, and a mock interview

faq.q: Is Cyient only for software roles?
faq.a: No. Cyient hires across many engineering branches (Mechanical, ECE, EEE, Aero, Civil, CS/IT, Telecom), so assessment content depends on the role.

faq.q: How do most freshers get in?
faq.a: Reports indicate campus drives are the main channel, with walk-ins and employee referrals also common.

faq.q: What does the online assessment cover?
faq.a: It varies by role: aptitude and logical reasoning plus either coding (software roles) or technical/domain questions (core roles).

name: Sonata Software
tagline: Runs a compact three-round process: an aptitude/technical/coding online test, a technical interview, and an HR round.
timeline: Online test → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: An online assessment covering aptitude, technical MCQs, and basic coding shortlists candidates for a technical interview (usually virtual) and an HR interview.

rounds.t: Aptitude (logical, quant, verbal), technical MCQs (C/Java/DBMS/OOP/OS), 1–2 basic coding problems
Core CS concepts, coding basics, projects (often virtual)
Communication, learning ability, fit

eligibility: No single published CGPA cutoff for all roles; strong academics, relevant skills, and project experience help. Confirm each drive's notification.
prep2: Days 1–3: Aptitude across logical, quant, and verbal
Days 4–6: Technical MCQ revision (C/Java/DBMS/OOP/OS)
Days 7–9: Basic coding practice
Days 10–12: Project prep and communication practice
Days 13–14: Full mock test plus mock technical and HR
prepC: Day 1: Timed aptitude plus technical MCQs and a few coding problems
Day 2: DBMS/OOP/OS revision, project prep, and a mock interview

faq.q: How many rounds does Sonata have?
faq.a: Reports describe a compact three-round process: an online assessment, a technical interview, and an HR interview.

faq.q: Is the coding difficult?
faq.a: No. The online test usually has one or two basic-level coding questions in a language like Java or Python.

faq.q: How do I avoid recruitment scams?
faq.a: Sonata never charges for recruitment. Verify communication comes from an @sonata-software.com address and use only the official careers page.

name: Nagarro
tagline: Coding-intensive hiring: a Mettl aptitude+coding test, a second pure-coding round (often graph/tree heavy), then technical and HR interviews.
timeline: Online test → interviews (2–4 weeks)
process: A Mettl-based test with aptitude, technical, and coding sections is followed by a second, tougher pure-coding round, then a technical interview (often optimizing your earlier code) and an HR round. Every round is elimination.

rounds.t: General aptitude, technical (OS/algorithms/DS/C/Java/SQL/networking), 3 coding problems
3–5 harder coding problems, often graphs/trees
Optimizing your earlier code, DSA, algorithms, SQL
Behavioral, resume-based, soft skills, fit

topics: Explaining and improving your own code
eligibility: Specific CGPA/percentage cutoffs vary by drive; because the process is coding-heavy, strong DSA matters more than a marginal cutoff. Confirm each drive's notification.
prep2: Days 1–2: Aptitude and reasoning refresh
Days 3–7: Intensive DSA daily (arrays, strings, recursion, then trees/graphs)
Days 8–10: Timed harder problems to simulate the second coding round
Days 11–12: OS/networking/SQL revision and code-optimization practice
Days 13–14: Two full timed coding mocks plus a mock technical and HR
prepC: Day 1: 12–15 medium problems focusing on trees and graphs under time
Day 2: Practice optimizing your own solutions, revise SQL/OS, and do a mock interview

faq.q: Why is Nagarro considered hard?
faq.a: The coding rounds are demanding, with the second round often featuring multiple graph/tree problems under tight time. Strong DSA is essential.

faq.q: What does the technical interview focus on?
faq.a: Interviewers commonly ask you to optimize the code you wrote in the second round, plus questions on DSA, algorithms, and SQL.

faq.q: Is every round elimination?
faq.a: Yes. You only get a call for the next round after clearing the current one, so treat each stage as a hard gate.

name: Google SWE
tagline: A first-principles coding loop that rewards clear reasoning over memorized patterns.
timeline: Recruiter → online assessment → phone screen → onsite loop → hiring committee (6–8 weeks)
process: One or two technical phone screens (medium/hard coding in a shared doc), then a virtual onsite of 4–6 rounds mixing coding, code comprehension, a Googleyness round, and (L5+) system design, ending with a central hiring committee and team match.

rounds.t: coding/DSA in a shared doc, spoken reasoning, complexity analysis
DSA: arrays, strings, trees/graphs, DP, recursion
reading, debugging and optimizing existing code (2026 pilot adds AI-assisted variants for some junior/mid roles)
HLD for L5+; scalability, data modeling, trade-offs
behavioral, collaboration, ambiguity, values

eligibility: open — role/level-based (L3 new grad through L5+), not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–4: drill arrays, strings, hashing and two pointers; solve out loud while writing complexity
Days 5–8: go deep on trees, graphs (BFS/DFS, topological, Dijkstra) and recursion
Days 9–11: dynamic programming patterns (knapsack, intervals, grid, LIS)
Days 12–13: practice reading and debugging unfamiliar code; if targeting L5+, do 2–3 system design mocks
Day 14: full timed mock in a plain doc, narrating your approach end to end
prepC: Day 1: 8–10 medium graph and DP problems, each explained aloud with complexity
Day 2: one hard problem, one debug-existing-code drill, and 3 Googleyness stories in STAR form

faq.q: How much do graphs and DP really matter?
faq.a: A lot. Google leans heavily on graph traversal and dynamic programming; being fluent there is one of the biggest levers on your outcome.

faq.q: What is the new code comprehension round?
faq.a: Announced as a 2026 pilot for select junior/mid US teams, it asks you to read, debug and optimize an existing codebase, sometimes with an AI assistant, testing prompting and output validation. Availability is limited, so confirm with your recruiter.

faq.q: Do I pick my team before or after interviews?
faq.a: Usually after. You pass a general loop and hiring committee first, then go through team matching, which can add time to the timeline.

name: Meta E5
tagline: A balanced loop where system design and behavioral often decide your level.
timeline: Recruiter → optional OA → phone screen → onsite loop (3–4 weeks)
process: After a recruiter call and possible online assessment, a coding phone screen (often 2 problems), then a full loop of coding rounds, a design round (system design for Infra, product architecture for Product), and a behavioral round that heavily influences whether you land E5 or get down-leveled.

rounds.t: coding/DSA, typically 2 medium problems with clean working code
DSA at pace, 2 problems per round; one round may be AI-enabled (2026 pilot)
system design (Infra) or product architecture (Product): scale, APIs, data model
ownership, conflict, impact; weighted heavily for leveling

topics: system design (news feed, messaging, rate limiter)
eligibility: E5 = senior IC (typically 5+ years); open, not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: grind Meta-tagged mediums, solving 2 in ~35 minutes with fully working code
Days 6–9: system design core (feed, chat, rate limiter, notifications) with clear data models and trade-offs
Days 10–12: write 6–8 STAR stories on impact, conflict and ownership scoped to senior scope
Day 13: full mock loop (2 coding + 1 design + 1 behavioral)
Day 14: review weak spots and rehearse concise complexity explanations
prepC: Day 1: 10 Meta-tagged mediums (2 at a time) plus one system design walkthrough
Day 2: refine 6 behavioral stories and do one timed design mock

faq.q: Can the behavioral round really down-level me?
faq.a: Yes. Meta uses behavioral signal strongly for leveling; a weak round can move an E5 candidate down to E4 even with solid coding.

faq.q: System design or product architecture?
faq.a: Depends on the role. Infrastructure candidates get system design; Product candidates get product architecture. Your recruiter tells you which.

faq.q: Is there an AI-assisted coding round?
faq.a: Meta is piloting one that replaces a coding round and expects you to show how you work with AI. It is not universal yet, so treat it as possible rather than guaranteed.

name: Microsoft SWE
tagline: A practical loop with approachable coding plus real low-level design.
timeline: OA → optional phone screen → onsite loop of 3–4 rounds (4–8 weeks)
process: After an online assessment (and sometimes a phone screen for experienced roles), a virtual loop on Teams with 3–4 one-hour rounds covering DSA coding, low-level/OOP design, system design for senior levels, and a behavioral or hiring-manager round.

rounds.t: DSA problems (LeetCode easy–medium) on CodeSignal/HackerRank
arrays, strings, hash maps, trees, linked lists, light DP
OOP modeling, clean class design, extensibility
HLD for experienced roles: components, scaling, trade-offs
hiring-manager or 'as-appropriate' round; judgment, collaboration

eligibility: open — role/level-based (SDE, SDE II, Senior); not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: LeetCode easy–medium across arrays, strings, hashing, trees and linked lists
Days 6–9: practice OOP/LLD (parking lot, elevator, card game) with clean classes and interfaces
Days 10–12: senior candidates add HLD basics (caching, queues, sharding, load balancing)
Day 13: mock loop of 2 coding + 1 LLD
Day 14: prepare hiring-manager stories and revisit complexity trade-offs
prepC: Day 1: 12 easy–medium DSA problems plus one LLD design
Day 2: one HLD walkthrough and 4 behavioral stories

faq.q: How hard is Microsoft's coding compared to Google?
faq.a: Generally easier. Problems skew easy-to-medium, so clean, correct, well-explained solutions matter more than cracking hard puzzles.

faq.q: Is there a low-level design round?
faq.a: Commonly yes. Microsoft frequently includes an OOP/LLD round, so practice modeling real objects with clean, extensible classes.

faq.q: Are interviews still remote?
faq.a: Most loops run virtually over Microsoft Teams, typically 3–4 one-hour rounds with peers, the hiring manager and sometimes a senior interviewer.

name: Apple SWE
tagline: A team-owned loop where each team writes its own questions and craft matters.
timeline: Recruiter + HM screen → tech screens → onsite loop (3–8 weeks)
process: The whole process sits inside the specific team you applied to: a recruiter and hiring-manager screen, one to three coding tech screens on CoderPad, then an onsite (often ~6 hours, sometimes two interviewers per session) of coding, system design for mid/senior, and a genuine 'Why Apple?' behavioral round.

rounds.t: background, role fit, motivation
DSA and language depth on CoderPad
HLD/LLD scoped to real Apple product constraints (mid/senior)
team-specific depth (systems, embedded, mobile, etc.)
'Why Apple?', collaboration, how you work

eligibility: open — team and role based; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: solid DSA plus deep fluency in the language the team uses
Days 6–8: research the specific team's domain and study its fundamentals
Days 9–11: system design scoped to Apple-style product and resource constraints
Days 12–13: build a real, specific 'Why Apple?' narrative and role-fit stories
Day 14: back-to-back mock rounds to build stamina for the long onsite
prepC: Day 1: 8–10 mediums in the team's language plus domain fundamentals review
Day 2: one design mock and a rehearsed 'Why Apple?' plus project deep-dives

faq.q: Is there a central question bank like Google or Meta?
faq.a: No. Each team owns its loop and writes its own questions, so the experience varies a lot by team and depth of your resume.

faq.q: How long is the onsite?
faq.a: Often around six hours of back-to-back interviews, and sometimes two interviewers question you at once, so pace and stamina matter.

faq.q: How much does 'Why Apple?' count?
faq.a: Meaningfully. Motivation and genuine product/craft interest come up throughout, not just in the behavioral round.

name: Adobe SWE
tagline: A fundamentals-first loop with real design depth for its product suite.
timeline: Recruiter → OA → coding rounds → design → HM close (3–6 weeks)
process: An online assessment (HackerRank/CodeSignal, sometimes with CS-fundamentals MCQs) leads into 2–3 DSA coding rounds, a system design round (HLD + LLD for mid/senior), and a hiring-manager or director behavioral close; roles are titled Computer Scientist / MTS in India.

rounds.t: 2–3 DSA problems, sometimes CS MCQs (OS, DBMS, networks)
DSA in C++/Java, clean code, complexity
HLD + LLD for mid/senior; design choices and trade-offs
behavioral, projects, product interest

eligibility: open — Computer Scientist 1/2 or MTS levels in India; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: DSA mediums in C++/Java with strong complexity discipline
Days 6–8: brush up OS, DBMS and networking fundamentals for the OA/MCQs
Days 9–11: practice HLD + LLD, explaining design choices out loud
Days 12–13: mock loop of 2 coding + 1 design
Day 14: prep hiring-manager stories and revisit weak topics
prepC: Day 1: 10 DSA mediums plus a fundamentals refresher
Day 2: one HLD/LLD walkthrough and 4 behavioral stories

faq.q: Which language should I use?
faq.a: C++ or Java are the common choices; interviewers value clean code and clear reasoning about design decisions.

faq.q: Does the OA test CS theory?
faq.a: Often yes. Adobe assessments frequently mix DSA with MCQs on OS, DBMS and networks, so review fundamentals alongside coding.

faq.q: How much design is there?
faq.a: Mid and senior candidates get a real design round covering both high-level and low-level design, weighing alternatives matters more than one perfect answer.

name: Salesforce SWE
tagline: A values-driven loop where culture fit weighs as much as coding.
timeline: Recruiter → HM → technical rounds → final panel (3–6 weeks)
process: A recruiter screen and hiring-manager round lead into technical interviews (live coding, often a HackerRank/CodeSignal assessment, and a system design session for relevant levels), closing with a panel round; values alignment is assessed at every stage.

rounds.t: background, motivation ('Why Salesforce?'), values fit
role fit, past work, expectations
DSA (LeetCode easy–medium, occasional hard, e.g. DFS)
HLD: scalability and reliability
behavioral tied to Salesforce values

eligibility: open — role/level-based; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: DSA mediums with focus on trees and graph traversal (DFS/BFS)
Days 6–9: HLD fundamentals (scalability, reliability, caching, queues)
Days 10–12: prepare values-based STAR stories and a strong 'Why Salesforce?'
Day 13: mock coding + design loop
Day 14: rehearse panel answers and clarify compensation expectations
prepC: Day 1: 10 DSA mediums (emphasis on DFS/graphs) plus one HLD walkthrough
Day 2: 5 values-mapped behavioral stories and a 'Why Salesforce?' pitch

faq.q: How important is culture fit?
faq.a: Very. Salesforce assesses values alignment at every stage and treats it as comparable in weight to technical skill.

faq.q: How hard is the coding?
faq.a: Mostly easy-to-medium, with occasional hard problems (candidates report DFS-heavy questions). Clean, correct solutions and clear communication matter.

faq.q: Is there an online assessment?
faq.a: Some candidates get a HackerRank-style assessment (reported as a NextGen Software Engineering Assessment) after the recruiter and hiring-manager screens; it is not universal.

name: Nvidia SWE
tagline: A deep-fundamentals loop where memory, performance and C++ depth are king.
timeline: Recruiter → OA → phone screens → HM → onsite loop (4–8 weeks)
process: A recruiter screen, often a HackerRank OA, one or two technical phone screens and a hiring-manager chat lead into an onsite of 3–5 rounds spanning coding or domain depth, performance-oriented system design, and a behavioral/experience round.

rounds.t: DSA problems on HackerRank (many roles)
C++/Python problem solving, complexity follow-ups
team's field from basics to advanced; OS, memory, concurrency
throughput, latency, memory; not generic CRUD
engineering judgment, fit with the team's work

eligibility: open — role/level-based (through principal); not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: DSA in C++ or Python with attention to time and space complexity
Days 6–9: study OS internals, memory hierarchy, caching and thread safety
Days 10–12: performance-focused design (latency, throughput, memory) plus your target team's domain
Day 13: mock coding + domain deep-dive
Day 14: prepare experience stories tied to engineering judgment
prepC: Day 1: 8–10 mediums plus an OS/memory/concurrency refresher
Day 2: one performance-oriented design mock and domain review for your team

faq.q: Do I need CUDA expertise?
faq.a: Usually not for general SWE, backend or infra roles. Strong algorithms, OS/Linux and C++/Python fundamentals matter far more, though specialized teams differ.

faq.q: What makes Nvidia's design round different?
faq.a: It centers on throughput, latency and memory rather than generic web-scale CRUD, expect follow-ups on cache performance and thread safety.

faq.q: How deep is the domain round?
faq.a: It moves from basic concepts to advanced, real-world application in the team's field, so know the fundamentals of the area you are interviewing for.

name: Uber SWE
tagline: A coding-forward loop themed around real-time, real-world infrastructure.
timeline: Recruiter → OA/coding screen → onsite loop of 3–5 rounds (4–6 weeks)
process: A recruiter screen, a CodeSignal OA (often ~4 problems) or live coding screen, then a virtual/onsite loop of 3–5 rounds; entry-level is coding-heavy while mid/senior add machine coding, system design and behavioral rounds emphasizing ownership.

rounds.t: ~4 algorithmic problems on CodeSignal (easy to hard)
live DSA on CodeSignal/Zoom
DSA and sometimes machine coding
trade-offs, scalability, latency (ride-matching, dispatch, surge)
ownership, cross-functional work, past impact

eligibility: open — role/level-based; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: DSA mediums/hards, especially graphs and DP, under time pressure
Days 6–9: system design of Uber-like problems (matching, dispatch, geospatial, surge)
Days 10–11: machine coding practice for mid/senior candidates
Days 12–13: mock loop of coding + design
Day 14: prepare ownership stories and revisit CodeSignal-style pacing
prepC: Day 1: one timed 4-problem CodeSignal-style set plus a graph/DP review
Day 2: one Uber-themed design mock (ride-matching or dispatch) and behavioral stories

faq.q: What is the online assessment like?
faq.a: Typically a CodeSignal test around 70–90 minutes with roughly four problems, mixing easy/medium array-string questions with harder graph or DP ones.

faq.q: What design topics come up?
faq.a: Problems mirror Uber's business: ride-matching engines, real-time location tracking, surge pricing and dispatch, with strong emphasis on latency and operational concerns.

faq.q: Is it coding-heavy for new grads?
faq.a: Yes. Entry-level loops are largely coding, while mid and senior candidates also face machine coding, system design and ownership-focused behavioral rounds.

name: Atlassian SWE
tagline: A build-a-real-thing loop with a values round that can make or break offers.
timeline: Recruiter → Karat screen → virtual onsite of 4–5 rounds (4–6 weeks)
process: A recruiter screen and a Karat technical screen (rapid-fire fundamentals plus 1–2 coding problems) lead into a virtual onsite of 4–5 rounds covering practical coding, system design and a heavily weighted values interview mapped to Atlassian's five values.

rounds.t: rapid-fire OS/networking basics plus 1–2 coding problems
build a real thing (game, report generator, feature flags) with follow-ups
HLD: multi-tenant/enterprise scale, trade-offs
behavioral mapped to Atlassian's five values (heavily weighted)
past work, code quality, practical judgment

topics: optimizing and scaling a built solution
eligibility: open — role/level-based; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–4: practice building small working programs (games, parsers, feature flags) end to end
Days 5–8: DSA mediums plus OS/networking quick-recall for the Karat screen
Days 9–11: HLD fundamentals with a lean toward multi-tenant/enterprise scenarios
Days 12–13: write STAR stories mapped to all five Atlassian values
Day 14: mock a build-a-thing coding round and a values interview
prepC: Day 1: two build-a-real-thing coding drills plus a fundamentals refresher
Day 2: 5 values-mapped stories and one HLD walkthrough

faq.q: What are Atlassian's five values?
faq.a: Open Company No Bullshit; Build with Heart and Balance; Don't #@!% the Customer; Play as a Team; and Be the Change You Seek. Prepare a story for each.

faq.q: Can I fail on values alone?
faq.a: Yes. Some candidates pass the technical rounds but are turned down over values or manager-fit, so treat that round as seriously as coding.

faq.q: How hard is the coding?
faq.a: Less LeetCode-hard, more 'build a real thing.' Expect to implement something like a snake game or feature-flag system and then optimize or scale it.

name: Walmart Global Tech
tagline: A practical loop pairing DSA with real design and STAR behavioral.
timeline: Recruiter → HackerRank OA → 2 technical rounds → HM round (4–6 weeks)
process: A recruiter screen with light technical questions, a one-hour HackerRank assessment (1–2 medium/hard problems, sometimes SQL), two technical rounds splitting DSA coding and design (LLD and HLD, sometimes separate at senior levels), and a conversational-but-behavioral hiring-manager round expecting STAR answers.

rounds.t: 1–2 medium/hard problems on HackerRank (Python and SQL appear)
data structures and algorithms, live coding
LLD and/or HLD; trade-offs and production reasoning
behavioral in STAR format, project deep-dives

eligibility: open — SE roles (SE III, senior, etc.) in Bengaluru/Chennai for India; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: DSA mediums plus a SQL refresher for the OA
Days 6–9: practice LLD (clean OOP) and HLD fundamentals
Days 10–12: prepare STAR stories and be ready to defend past architecture decisions
Day 13: mock loop of 1 coding + 1 design
Day 14: rehearse hiring-manager answers on trade-offs and impact
prepC: Day 1: 10 DSA mediums plus SQL practice
Day 2: one LLD and one HLD walkthrough, plus 4 STAR stories

faq.q: Does the OA include SQL?
faq.a: It can. The HackerRank assessment has 1–2 medium/hard problems and both Python and SQL have shown up, so brush up on SQL.

faq.q: How much design is there?
faq.a: Meaningful. One technical round centers on design, low-level and high-level both appear, and senior loops may split them into separate rounds.

faq.q: What is the hiring-manager round like?
faq.a: Conversational in tone but behavioral in substance. Bring STAR-format stories and be ready to explain what you built and why.

name: Flipkart
tagline: A loop known for its distinctive hands-on machine coding round.
timeline: OA → DSA round → machine coding → system design → managerial/HR (3–4 weeks)
process: An online coding assessment leads into a live DSA round, Flipkart's signature machine coding round (build a working, extensible system), a system design round for SDE-2 and above, and a managerial plus HR conversation.

rounds.t: 2–3 DSA problems (medium/hard) on HackerRank/HackerEarth
data structures and algorithms, live coding
build a working system with clean OOP and extensibility
HLD for SDE-2+; schema, scale, trade-offs
ownership, fit, compensation

topics: machine coding (Splitwise, ride-matching, LRU, booking systems)
eligibility: open — SDE-1 through SDE-3+; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: DSA mediums/hards across arrays, strings, DP, graphs and trees
Days 6–9: practice machine coding (Splitwise, parking lot, booking, LRU) with clean, extensible OOP
Days 10–12: system design for SDE-2+ (schema design, scaling a product like Twitter)
Day 13: timed machine coding mock plus a DSA round
Day 14: prepare ownership stories and review complexity
prepC: Day 1: one full machine-coding build (e.g. Splitwise) plus 8 DSA mediums
Day 2: one system design walkthrough and behavioral prep

faq.q: What is the machine coding round?
faq.a: A timed session where you build a working, modular system (Splitwise-style splitter, ride-matching, booking, LRU cache) graded on working code, clean OOP and extensibility. It is a defining filter at Flipkart.

faq.q: When does system design kick in?
faq.a: From SDE-2 upward. Expect to design a minimal version of a real product and discuss schema and queries.

faq.q: How fast is the process?
faq.a: Fairly quick, often 21–30 days across 4–5 rounds.

name: Swiggy
tagline: A DSA-strong loop where low-level design is the real filter.
timeline: OA → 2–3 tech rounds → bar-raiser/managerial → HR (2–6 weeks, ~24 days avg)
process: An online coding assessment (3 problems in ~60–90 min for DSA roles) leads into 2–3 technical rounds mixing DSA and low-level design, then a bar-raiser/managerial round and an HR conversation; LLD consistently trips up strong coders.

rounds.t: 3 medium DSA problems on HackerRank
2 mediums (arrays, intervals) plus language basics
low-level/OOP design, the key filter
system design and ownership; hiring-manager round
fit and compensation

eligibility: open — SDE-1 through SDE-2+; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: DSA mediums (arrays, intervals, sliding window, hashing)
Days 6–9: dedicated low-level design practice (this is where many candidates fail)
Days 10–12: system design for senior roles plus Java/backend fundamentals
Day 13: mock loop of 1 DSA + 1 LLD
Day 14: ownership stories and complexity review
prepC: Day 1: 10 DSA mediums plus one LLD design
Day 2: one system design walkthrough and behavioral prep

faq.q: What is the hardest round?
faq.a: Low-level design. Candidates who ace DSA still get rejected here, so treat LLD as a first-class prep area.

faq.q: What does the OA look like?
faq.a: Usually three medium DSA problems in 60–90 minutes on HackerRank; full-stack roles may instead build a CRUD app over ~3 hours.

faq.q: How long is the whole process?
faq.a: Around 24 days on average, though it can range from 2 to 6 weeks depending on scheduling.

name: Zomato
tagline: A lean-engineering loop from OA to a Gurgaon culture-fit round.
timeline: OA → DSA + projects → design + core CS → culture fit → HR (3–5 rounds)
process: An online assessment (2–3 medium/hard DSA problems plus debugging) leads into a DSA-and-projects round, a design-and-core-CS round (HLD/LLD plus OS/DB/networks), a culture-fit managerial round often held at Zomato's Gurgaon HQ, and a short HR call.

rounds.t: 2–3 medium/hard DSA problems plus debugging
DSA plus a deep dive into your past projects
HLD/LLD plus OS, DB and networking fundamentals
ownership, customer focus, lean-engineering values (often onsite in Gurgaon)
compensation, timelines

eligibility: open — SDE roles; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: DSA mediums (arrays, hashing, recursion, sliding window) plus debugging drills
Days 6–8: revise OS, DBMS and networking fundamentals
Days 9–11: HLD/LLD practice and be ready to defend your project decisions
Day 13: mock loop of 1 DSA + 1 design
Day 14: prepare culture-fit stories on ownership and customer focus
prepC: Day 1: 10 DSA mediums plus a core-CS refresher
Day 2: one design walkthrough and project-defense prep

faq.q: What does Zomato look for beyond code?
faq.a: Alignment with ownership, customer focus and lean engineering. The culture-fit round carries real weight and is often held onsite in Gurgaon.

faq.q: How deep are the CS fundamentals?
faq.a: Expect real questions on OS, DBMS and networking alongside DSA, so do not skip fundamentals.

faq.q: How is the coding graded?
faq.a: On clean, production-ready style, not just passing tests. Clarity and edge-case handling matter.

name: PhonePe
tagline: An eliminatory fintech loop pairing machine coding with hard DSA.
timeline: Machine coding → DSA → system design → hiring manager (2–4 weeks)
process: Typically four eliminatory rounds: a take-home-style machine coding round (problem sent, code submitted as a zip), a hard DSA round where you must fully solve at least two of three problems, a fintech-flavored system design round, and a hiring-manager round with senior payments leaders.

rounds.t: build a working system, submit as a zip; clean modular code
3 medium/hard problems; solve at least 2 fully to pass
fintech scenarios (e.g. real-time order feed, payment flows)
ownership, project clarity; often EM plus a payments head

eligibility: open — SDE-1 through SDE-3+; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–4: machine coding practice, building clean modular systems end to end
Days 5–9: hard DSA, focused on fully passing all test cases under time
Days 10–12: fintech system design (order feeds, payment flows, real-time updates)
Day 13: timed machine coding mock
Day 14: prepare ownership and project-clarity stories
prepC: Day 1: one full machine-coding build plus 8 medium/hard DSA problems
Day 2: one fintech system design mock and behavioral prep

faq.q: How does the machine coding round work?
faq.a: You get a problem, code a working solution (about 1.5 hours of effort, sometimes within a 24-hour window) and submit it as a zip. Clean, modular, extensible code is the goal.

faq.q: What is the DSA bar?
faq.a: High. You typically face three medium-to-hard problems and need to fully solve at least two, all test cases passing, to advance.

faq.q: Are the rounds eliminatory?
faq.a: Yes. Each round is a gate, so you must clear one to reach the next.

name: Paytm
tagline: A fintech loop with two DSA gates plus wallet-flavored LLD and HLD.
timeline: OA → 2 DSA rounds → machine coding/LLD → system design (2–4 weeks)
process: An online assessment leads into two live DSA rounds (the second, harder one is an elimination gate), a machine-coding/LLD round building a fintech feature, and a domain-specific system design round on flows like UPI and transactions.

rounds.t: 2–3 coding problems (easy–hard), sometimes 1 SQL
2 LeetCode mediums, clean code, complexity
harder problem (stacks, heaps, DP, monotonic); elimination
build a fintech feature (wallet, cashback, statement); SOLID/OOP
domain-specific (UPI flows, transactions, Soundbox)

eligibility: open — SDE-2 and senior levels; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: DSA mediums plus harder stack/heap/DP/monotonic problems
Days 6–9: machine coding/LLD with SOLID principles on fintech features
Days 10–12: HLD for UPI/transaction flows and fintech data modeling
Day 13: mock loop of 2 DSA + 1 LLD
Day 14: revisit weak areas and rehearse design trade-offs
prepC: Day 1: 10 DSA problems (incl. harder stacks/heaps/DP) plus one LLD build
Day 2: one UPI/transaction HLD walkthrough

faq.q: Which DSA round is the elimination gate?
faq.a: The second, harder live coding round, often stacks, heaps, advanced DP or monotonic structures, tends to be the make-or-break filter.

faq.q: What machine coding problems come up?
faq.a: Fintech features like a Paytm Wallet, cashback engine or mini-statement, graded on SOLID principles, clean code and extensibility.

faq.q: What design topics are common?
faq.a: Domain-specific ones: UPI payment flows, the bank transaction system and Paytm Soundbox recur in HLD rounds.

name: Razorpay
tagline: A fintech loop that indexes hard on machine coding and past project judgment.
timeline: Recruiter → OA → machine coding → system design + HM → HR (2–4 weeks)
process: A recruiter screen, a proctored OA (2–3 DSA plus MCQs, recently including AI/LLM basics), a machine-coding/LLD round building a modular system, and system design plus hiring-manager rounds that dig deep into your past projects and architecture decisions.

rounds.t: 2–3 DSA problems plus MCQs (incl. AI/LLM concepts recently)
build a modular system (load balancer, pub-sub); clean OOP
HLD plus resume/project deep-dive
architecture decisions, judgment, ownership
fit and compensation

eligibility: open — SDE-1 through senior; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–4: DSA mediums plus a quick review of AI/LLM basics for the OA MCQs
Days 5–9: machine coding/LLD (load balancer, pub-sub, end-to-end flows) with clean OOP
Days 10–12: HLD practice and prepare detailed walkthroughs of your past projects
Day 13: timed machine coding mock
Day 14: rehearse architecture-decision stories and failure-mode reasoning
prepC: Day 1: one machine-coding build plus 8 DSA mediums
Day 2: one HLD walkthrough and detailed project deep-dive prep

faq.q: What does the machine coding round test?
faq.a: Building a functional, modular system from scratch, examples include load balancers and pub-sub workflows, with clean, extensible code.

faq.q: Why do they dig into my past projects?
faq.a: Razorpay treats prior work as evidence of engineering judgment, so expect resume deep-dives and questions on why you built things a certain way.

faq.q: Does the OA cover AI topics?
faq.a: Recent assessments have added MCQs on AI fundamentals and LLM concepts alongside DSA, so skim those basics.

name: Zoho
tagline: A multi-level programming gauntlet from aptitude to a full app build.
timeline: Aptitude → basic programming → advanced/app build → technical → HR (4–5 rounds)
process: A staged, elimination-based process for freshers: an aptitude and programming-tracing test, a basic programming round, an advanced programming round where you build a small working application over a few hours, a technical interview walking through your code and CS fundamentals, and an HR round.

rounds.t: aptitude plus C/Java code tracing (often pen-and-paper, offline)
3+ problems on arrays, strings, patterns, number logic in a plain editor
build a small app (reservation, inventory, parking lot) with clean modular code
walk through your app, OOP, DBMS basics, problem variations
intent, relocation (often Chennai), long-term fit

eligibility: primarily freshers/new grads; role-based, not strictly CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–3: aptitude drills and C/Java code-tracing practice
Days 4–7: pattern, string and number-logic problems in a plain editor
Days 8–11: build 2–3 small apps (parking lot, inventory, reservation) with clean modular code
Days 12–13: review OOP and DBMS basics and be ready to explain your code
Day 14: mock technical interview walking through a built app
prepC: Day 1: aptitude + code tracing plus a batch of pattern/string problems
Day 2: build one small app end to end and review OOP/DBMS basics

faq.q: How is Zoho different from typical LeetCode loops?
faq.a: It emphasizes building small working applications and pattern/logic problems in a plain editor over heavy algorithmic puzzles, with an early aptitude and code-tracing gate.

faq.q: Is relocation expected?
faq.a: Often yes. The HR round commonly discusses relocating to Chennai (or another campus), so be ready to talk about it.

faq.q: Are the rounds eliminatory?
faq.a: Yes, it is a staged gauntlet, each level filters candidates before the next.

name: Freshworks
tagline: A SaaS-focused loop of DSA, LLD, HLD and hiring manager.
timeline: DSA → LLD → HLD → hiring manager (3–4 eliminatory rounds)
process: Typically four eliminatory rounds, a DSA coding assessment/interview, a low-level design round, a high-level system design round, and a hiring-manager round, with interviewers probing CS fundamentals and SaaS product sense throughout.

rounds.t: 3 medium/hard problems (often a home assessment first)
OOP modeling, clean extensible classes
HLD: DB internals, APIs, rate limiting, trade-offs
behavioral, project architecture, product sense

eligibility: open — SDE through lead levels; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: DSA mediums/hards for the coding assessment
Days 6–8: LLD practice with clean, extensible OOP
Days 9–11: HLD fundamentals (APIs, rate limiting, DB internals, caching)
Days 12–13: mock loop of 1 DSA + 1 design and prepare project stories
Day 14: review CS fundamentals and trade-off reasoning
prepC: Day 1: 10 DSA mediums plus one LLD design
Day 2: one HLD walkthrough (e.g. rate limiter) and behavioral prep

faq.q: How many rounds are there?
faq.a: Usually four eliminatory rounds, DSA, LLD, HLD and hiring manager, though some candidates see a compressed three-round version.

faq.q: What do the design rounds reward?
faq.a: Reasoning about alternatives and trade-offs, not just one working answer. Design internals and API principles come up often.

faq.q: Does product sense matter?
faq.a: Yes. Since you would build a live SaaS product, interviewers probe CS fundamentals and how you think about real customers.

name: Airbnb SWE
tagline: A rigorous loop pairing hard DP with a weighty Core Values round.
timeline: Recruiter → technical screen → onsite loop of 4–5 rounds (2–5 weeks)
process: A recruiter screen, a technical screen (live coding on CoderPad or an automated assessment, fully working code required), then a virtual onsite of 4–5 rounds spanning coding, system design, a code review round, and one or two Core Values interviews that genuinely affect the decision.

rounds.t: live coding on CoderPad (working code, no pseudocode)
DSA including hard dynamic programming
architecture reasoning; reliability, performance, UX
reading and critiquing code for quality and correctness
mission alignment, ownership; weighted in the decision

eligibility: open — role/level-based; not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–5: DSA with a heavy emphasis on hard dynamic programming
Days 6–9: system design focused on reliability, performance and user experience
Days 10–11: practice code review, spotting bugs and quality issues in given code
Days 12–13: prepare genuine Core Values / mission-alignment stories
Day 14: full mock loop with fully working code (no pseudocode)
prepC: Day 1: 8–10 hard DP problems plus one system design walkthrough
Day 2: one code review drill and Core Values story prep

faq.q: How hard is the coding?
faq.a: Rigorous, with a reputation for hard dynamic programming. Fully working code is required, pseudocode is not accepted.

faq.q: How much do Core Values count?
faq.a: A lot. The Core Values interview carries real weight in the decision, and recruiters listen for mission alignment from the first call.

faq.q: Is there a code review round?
faq.a: Yes, typically. The onsite often includes reading and critiquing code, so practice evaluating quality and correctness, not just writing code.

name: CRED
tagline: A craft-heavy fintech loop that indexes on development skill over LeetCode.
timeline: Take-home → DSA + puzzles → machine coding → system design + managerial
process: Roughly four rounds: a 24-hour take-home assignment, a practical DSA-and-puzzles round, a long machine-coding/LLD round, and a system design plus managerial round with the head of engineering focused on fintech-grade concerns.

rounds.t: build a POC (often clean-architecture, feature-rich) and share the codebase
2 practical mediums (sliding window, maps, sets, heaps) plus puzzles
clean, modular, extensible design (LRU, key-value store, game systems)
fintech design (idempotency, dedup, failure cases) with head of engineering

topics: machine coding / LLD and design patterns
eligibility: open — SDE-1 through SDE-2+ (and interns); not CGPA-gated
prep2: Days 1–4: sharpen practical DSA (sliding window, maps, sets, heaps) plus a few puzzles
Days 5–9: machine coding/LLD with design patterns (LRU, key-value store, game systems)
Days 10–12: fintech system design (idempotency, dedup, failure modes, schema at scale)
Day 13: timed machine coding mock plus a take-home-style build
Day 14: review clean architecture and tooling fluency
prepC: Day 1: one machine-coding build with clean patterns plus practical DSA drills
Day 2: one fintech system design mock (idempotency, dedup, failures)

faq.q: How is CRED different from big-tech loops?
faq.a: It indexes on development skill and general tooling outside the big-tech ecosystem, machine coding, clean architecture and practical judgment matter more than LeetCode-hard puzzles.

faq.q: What does the machine coding round test?
faq.a: Low-level design, building clean, modular, extensible solutions like LRU caches, key-value stores or game systems, with good design patterns, error handling and passing tests.

faq.q: What does the system design round emphasize?
faq.a: Fintech-grade concerns: idempotency to prevent duplicate transactions, data deduplication, failure handling and schema design feasible at CRED's scale.
